title: Deutsche Bank Rolls Out Agentic AI for Wealth Checks in Asia
excerpt: Tuesday, 22 September 2026. Finance >. Deutsche Bank Rolls Out Agentic AI for Wealth Checks in Asia. Yiping Li, chief operating officer of Deutsche Bank Private Bank. (Image: courtesy). FINANCE Tuesday, 22 September 2026 13:25 Deutsche Bank Rolls Out Agentic AI for Wealth Checks in Asia. " rel="nofollow">. PDF. Deutsche Bank Rolls Out Agentic AI for Wealth Checks in Asia. Deutsche Bank Private Bank has introduced an agentic AI tool in Singapore and Hong Kong to support source-of-wealth checks, as it prepares for higher client onboarding volumes. The solution went live at the bank’s Singapore and Hong Kong booking centres in early September, Deutsche Bank said in a statement on Tuesday. It has also been introduced for advisers in Dubai handling accounts booked in Singapore. A broader rollout across the Private Bank’s wealth management centres is planned. The tool automates research, documentation and the preparation of source-of-wealth data. These checks form a core part of the know-your-customer (KYC) process, requiring banks to establish how prospective clients accumulated their wealth. Human Oversight. Integrated into Deutsche Bank’s digital KYC platform, the solution analyses client documents and information from approved external sources. It helps identify gaps or inconsistencies and prepares source-of-wealth assessments for human review. «We developed it with a clear principle in mind: while tasks can be automated, accountability remains with our people,» said Yiping Li , chief operating officer of Deutsche Bank Private Bank. The bank said the tool would reduce administrative work and allow relationship managers to spend more time advising clients, while retaining its existing control framework. Higher Onboarding Volumes. Deutsche Bank expects the solution to support significantly higher onboarding volumes. Based on current forecasts, its Emerging Markets coverage region is on track to onboard approximately 30 percent more clients in 2026 than in 2025. The figure is a regional forecast, rather than a measure of gains already delivered by the AI tool. The bank also said the initiative supports Singapore’s wealth management industry ambition to achieve median client onboarding times of one month or less, including more complex cases. Marco Pagliara , head of Emerging Markets at Deutsche Bank Private Bank, said reducing repetitive tasks would help relationship managers focus on advice while improving the quality and consistency of the bank’s processes. title: ISO 42001 May Become a Payments AI Governance Benchmark
excerpt: ISO 42001 May Become a Payments AI Governance Benchmark. --> By PYMNTS | September 21, 2026. Share: --> |. Highlights. ISO 42001 sets requirements for establishing and maintaining an AI management system. FSS and Axis Bank provide recent examples of the standard being applied in payments and banking. Third-party AI could make ISO 42001 relevant to payments procurement, particularly as financial institutions scrutinize vendors’ AI governance. Payments firms need a way to identify where artificial intelligence is being used and who’s responsible for it, as well as to monitor how those systems are managed over time. ISO/IEC 42001 puts a management framework around those systems, including AI a company buys rather than builds. Published in December 2023, the standard establishes requirements for an AI management system, or AIMS. It applies to organizations that develop, provide or use AI products and services and covers the establishment, implementation, maintenance and continual improvement of the management system. The intent is to govern how an organization manages AI throughout its lifecycle. At a high level, the standard addresses responsibility, risk assessment, monitoring and other management processes rather than setting technical performance requirements for individual fraud, authentication or underwriting models. For payments companies, implementing ISO 42001 can start with finding the AI already operating inside the business. “The biggest change is that it makes firms take a much closer look at where AI is actually being used,” Christian Jacob , a financial crime and AI governance professional with payments experience, told PYMNTS. That includes machine-learning components inside fraud detection, transaction monitoring, onboarding, authentication and other decisioning workflows, Jacob said. The review can uncover systems that previously had been treated simply as operational technology. Jacob, who works at Deel , told PYMNTS his comments were being provided in a personal capacity. Identifying those systems is one issue. Responsibility after deployment is another. David Kemmerer , co-founder and CEO of CoinLedger , told PYMNTS separately that payments companies may already have established processes for security, fraud, privacy, model risk and compliance. The problem can emerge after an AI system has entered production. “The tough bit is who owns an AI system after deployment or the governance of changes in the model,” Kemmerer said. “ISO 42001 provides coverage for creation, implementation, maintenance and improvements. ”. The requirement for continuing oversight is significant because AI systems can change in effectiveness as data, behavior and operating conditions change. Management of the system therefore continues after its initial approval. When AI Touches the Transaction. Rustam Bagautdinov, director of processing at Payzon , pointed to payment routing as an example of where the issue reaches transaction processing. AI can be used to select an acquiring route using variables such as expected approval rates and cost. A change in the model’s behavior can therefore alter where transactions are sent. “If an AI suddenly routes a batch of cross-border transactions through a path that triggers massive false declines, ISO 42001 ensures there is a traceable, documented logic to understand why the model made that choice, rather than just blaming the algorithm,” Bagautdinov said. The example illustrates the operational purpose of governance without turning certification into a performance guarantee. ISO 42001 does not determine whether an individual routing decision is correct. It requires management processes around AI systems within the organization’s defined scope. The Standard Reaches Outside the Company. Payments companies also depend on technology they do not own. Fraud detection, screening, onboarding and authentication can be supplied by third parties. title: Panic over AI puts Spanish banking plans in check after redesigning their models to adapt to the new technology
excerpt: NEWS. Panic over AI puts Spanish banking plans in check after redesigning their models to adapt to the new technology. MAR�A HERN�NDEZ. Updated 09/21/2026 - 04:15 ET. Share on Facebook. Share on X. Send by email. Entities are moving between caution and uncertainty due to the impact that the crisis of confidence in artificial intelligence can have on their businesses. The emergence of Mythos, Anthropic's AI model, caused a global earthquake that activated alarms in the financial sector in Europe and in Spain. That episode, which led to the regional banks being called to action by the ECB, could be just a footnote compared to the alerts being issued in recent days by the major leaders in artificial intelligence, sparking a global panic. If the development of the new technology could end humanity, what could it not do to the entities?. For now, the crisis of confidence triggered by the messages from Dario Amodei, Sam Altman, or Elon Musk is putting the strategic plans of the main Spanish entities at risk, which have placed artificial intelligence at the core of their operating models and are in the process of implementing the technology in their structures and business models. They are all closely monitoring the clash of opinions between those advocating for slowing down the pace of advancements and those, like US President Donald Trump or Meta's CEO, Mark Zuckerberg , rejecting that idea. One of the listed entities in Spain acknowledges that there is concern in the sector about the impact of this crisis, not so much because the banks here have direct exposure, but because of their financing to other companies in the Ibex 35 that have already requested capital to develop data center hubs in the United States. "If there were a crisis in support of AI investments in the United States, that would worry us," they admit. Therefore, caution is the prevailing attitude among the major banks. They believe that the debate is taking place at a different level than theirs, dominated by technology companies and investors with interests in those companies, and argue that banks, like companies in other sectors, simply decide what to do or how to implement developments that are given to them. Nevertheless, reflection processes in the top management of the entities are underway, and everyone is working to anticipate responses to possible incidents following the guidelines set by the European Central Bank. Following the appearance of Mythos, the regulator requested contingency plans and analysis of digital vulnerabilities from regional entities. In July, the regulator increased surveillance and sent a letter to European banks urging them to rethink their cybersecurity models. For this purpose, the text specified: "Where appropriate, this approach [cybersecurity] could be complemented by the use of AI-based tools, provided that their implementation is preceded by a thorough assessment of both their potential benefits and associated risks, and subject to appropriate safeguards, human oversight, and robust risk management. ". Since then, Spanish banks - and European ones as well - are aligning their defense mechanisms to the new risks posed by AI. Industry sources explain that cybersecurity plans include two forms of defense: on one hand, the traditional one, which basically involves bolstering security measures , updating software patches. And on the other hand, a defense based on the controlled use of AI, with risk assessment protocols, limiting its autonomy, and under continuous human supervision. "Attacks are mainly aimed at the patches applied to the software and vulnerability management. The most targeted companies will be those that do not apply software patches as they are released," they share with EL MUNDO. The institution chaired by Christine Lagarde demanded that banks have their action programs against artificial intelligence ready by October 31.
